function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL and retrieves data as specified by the parameters. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. It is expected to be a well-formed HTTP or HTTPS URL.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: A dictionary of HTTP headers to send with the request. Each key-value pair represents a header name and its value.

timeout.description: The number of seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, as a float, or a (connect_timeout, read_timeout) tuple. This is a float type value.

lat.description: Latitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

lon.description: Longitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters to append to the URL for the GET request.

allow_redirects.description: Determines if HTTP redirections (301, 302, etc.) should be followed.

auth.description: A tuple representing the user credentials for HTTP authentication, typically in the form of (username, password).

cert.description: Path to an SSL certificate file to verify the peer, or a tuple of (certificate file, key file).

cookies.description: A dictionary of cookies to send with the request. The key is the cookie name and the value is the cookie value.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: A dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy.

stream.description: If True, the response content will not be downloaded immediately but streamed.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not, or a path to a CA bundle if verification is needed.

message.content:
When you’re tracking currency valuations (e.g., exchange rates, price indices, or any time‑series data that changes daily, hourly, or even tick‑by‑tick), you want a structure that: 1. **Keeps data sorted by time** – so you can quickly find the most recent value or interpolate between points. 2. **Supports fast inserts and updates** – because new rates arrive continuously. 3. **Allows efficient range queries** – e.g., “give me all rates between 2023‑01‑01 and 2023‑01‑31”. 4. **Handles sparse data gracefully** – many currencies may have missing days or irregular intervals. Below are the most common data structures that satisfy these needs, along with their trade‑offs and typical use cases. | Data Structure | Typical Use Case | Strengths | Weaknesses | When to Prefer | |----------------|------------------|-----------|------------|----------------| | **Array / List of tuples** (`[(timestamp, value), …]`) | Small datasets, offline analysis, simple scripts | • Very fast random access (O(1))
• Simple to implement | • Insertion/deletion O(n)
• Requires sorting after each insert if unsorted | • When data size is small (< 10 k rows) or you can batch‑load sorted data | | **Sorted Array / List** (`sortedcontainers.SortedList` in Python) | Medium‑size datasets, need binary search | • Binary search O(log n)
• Maintains order automatically | • Insert/delete O(log n) + shift O(n) | • When you need sorted order and moderate updates | | **Balanced BST / TreeMap** (`std::map`, `TreeMap` in Java, `BTree` in SQLite) | Large datasets, frequent inserts/updates | • O(log n) insert, delete, search
• Keeps data sorted | • Memory overhead for pointers
• Slightly slower than array for pure reads | • When you need real‑time updates and range queries | | **Skip List** | Concurrent environments, need probabilistic balancing | • O(log n) operations
• Easier to implement lock‑free variants | • Randomized performance
• Slightly higher memory | • When you need concurrent reads/writes without heavy locking | | **Time‑Series Database (TSDB)** (`InfluxDB`, `TimescaleDB`, `Prometheus`) | Production systems, high‑volume streams | • Built‑in compression, retention policies
• Efficient downsampling & aggregation
• Query language (SQL/Flux) | • Requires external service
• Overkill for simple apps | • When you need long‑term storage, high ingestion rates, and advanced analytics | | **Key‑Value Store with Time‑Index** (`Redis`, `Cassandra`, `DynamoDB`) | Distributed systems, need horizontal scaling | • Extremely fast writes/reads
• Can shard by key | • Requires custom logic for range queries | • When you need massive scale and can tolerate eventual consistency | | **Columnar Store** (`Parquet`, `ORC`) | Batch analytics, OLAP | • Excellent compression
• Column‑wise scans | • Not ideal for real‑time inserts | • When you do heavy analytical queries on historical data | ### Recommendation for Most Use Cases | Scenario | Suggested Structure | Why | |----------|---------------------|-----| | **Small to medium app (≤ 100 k rows)** | `sortedcontainers.SortedList` (Python) or `TreeMap` (Java) | Keeps data sorted, fast inserts, no external dependency | | **High‑frequency trading / real‑time feeds** | In‑memory `Skip List` or `BTree` + optional `Redis` cache | Handles concurrent updates, low latency | | **Long‑term archival + analytics** | TimescaleDB (PostgreSQL extension) or InfluxDB | Built‑in retention, downsampling, powerful SQL | | **Distributed microservices** | Cassandra + secondary index on timestamp | Scales horizontally, fault tolerant | ### Practical Example (Python) ```python from sortedcontainers import SortedList from datetime import datetime # Each entry is a tuple: (timestamp, value) rates = SortedList(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Insert a new rate rates.add((datetime.utcnow(), 1.2345)) # Find the most recent rate most_recent = rates[-1] # Get all rates in a date range start, end = datetime(2023, 1, 1), datetime(2023, 1, 31) idx_start = rates.bisect_left((start,)) idx_end = rates.bisect_right((end,)) jan_rates = rates[idx_start:idx_end] ``` ### Things to Keep in Mind 1. **Indexing** – If you store data in a relational DB, create an index on the timestamp column for fast range queries. 2. **Compression** – For long‑term storage, consider delta‑encoding or run‑length encoding to reduce disk usage. 3. **Retention Policies** – Decide how long you keep raw data vs. aggregated snapshots (e.g., daily averages). 4. **Time‑Zone Normalization** – Store timestamps in UTC to avoid ambiguity. 5. **Precision** – Use `Decimal` or fixed‑point types for financial calculations to avoid floating‑point errors. --- **Bottom line:** For most applications that need a mix of real‑time updates and efficient range queries, a **balanced BST (e.g., `TreeMap` or `BTree`) or a sorted list with binary search** is the sweet spot. If you anticipate very high write throughput or need distributed scaling, move to a **TSDB** or **distributed KV store**. If you’re just prototyping or dealing with a small dataset, a plain **sorted array** or **list** will do fine.
